topics.title: Union Budget 2026-27: Sitharaman's ninth budget targets a 4.3% deficit
topics.hook: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman presented her ninth consecutive Union Budget on February 1, 2026, pushing capital spending up while trimming the fiscal deficit target to 4.3% of GDP.
topics.story:
Nirmala Sitharaman stood up in the Lok Sabha on February 1, 2026, a Sunday, to read her ninth Budget speech in a row, more consecutive budgets than any Finance Minister before her. The government pegged total expenditure at Rs 53,47,315 crore for 2026-27, a 7.7% jump over the previous year, while non-debt receipts were projected at Rs 36.5 lakh crore. The headline number for a CLAT aspirant to remember is the fiscal deficit target: 4.3% of GDP, down from 4.4% in 2025-26, continuing the glide path the government has followed since the pandemic blew the deficit past 9% in 2020-21.

Capital expenditure rose to Rs 12.2 lakh crore, the government's preferred lever for growth because money spent on roads, ports and railways is supposed to crowd in private investment rather than just fund consumption. Total public debt stood at 55.6% of GDP, a number the government cites to show it has room left before debt becomes a drag on growth, unlike Sri Lanka in 2022 or Pakistan's recurring IMF bailouts.

The Budget's technology spine was India Semiconductor Mission 2.0, cleared by the Expenditure Finance Committee at an overall outlay of Rs 1.25 lakh crore against Rs 76,000 crore for the first phase, with a budgetary provision of Rs 1,000 crore for FY27 alone plus Rs 8,000 crore for the associated Modified Programme for semiconductor and display manufacturing. The idea is to move India from assembling chips to designing and fabricating them, reducing the import dependence that a taxing paper might frame as a supply-chain vulnerability. The Budget also launched Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 with a Rs 10,000 crore corpus aimed at non-metro founders, and proposed a High Level Committee on Banking for Viksit Bharat.

A day earlier, on January 29, the Chief Economic Adviser had tabled the Economic Survey 2025-26 projecting real GDP growth of 7.4% for the current year and a range of 6.8% to 7.2% for 2026-27, numbers Sitharaman leaned on to argue that India remains the fastest-growing large economy even as the United States and China slow.

Constitutionally, the Budget is the Annual Financial Statement under Article 112, the document that lays before Parliament the estimated receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year. No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India, under Article 266, except under appropriation made by law, which is why the Finance Bill and Appropriation Bill that follow the speech matter as much as the speech itself. The Railway Budget, presented separately every year from 1924, was merged into the general Budget starting 2017, so railway allocations now sit inside the same document Sitharaman read on February 1.

For an exam, the trap is treating the Budget as a single number question. Examiners are more likely to test the mechanism: what Article 112 actually says, why a fiscal deficit target matters, or how capital expenditure differs from revenue expenditure in its effect on growth.

topics.title: India AI Impact Summit 2026 and the New Delhi Declaration
topics.hook: India hosted the AI Impact Summit at Bharat Mandapam from February 16 to 21, 2026, and 92 countries and organisations signed the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact.
topics.story:
The AI Impact Summit ran for six days at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi, drawing roughly six lakh in-person attendees and more than nine lakh cumulative views on its livestream. On February 19, 2026, the summit adopted the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact, initially endorsed by 89 countries and international organisations, a number that grew to 92 as more signatories joined over the following days. The Declaration draws its framing from two Sanskrit phrases: Sarvajan Hitaya, Sarvajan Sukhaya, meaning welfare and happiness for all, and Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, the world is one family, both invoked to argue that AI's gains cannot stay concentrated among a handful of rich countries.

The text organises itself around seven pillars it calls Chakras, covering democratised access to AI resources, economic growth, secure and trusted systems, scientific research, social empowerment, human capital development, and energy-efficient AI. Concrete initiatives flowed from these pillars: a Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI meant to give developing countries affordable access to foundational models and compute, a Global AI Impact Commons to share use cases, a Trusted AI Commons offering benchmarking tools, and an International Network of AI for Science Institutions.

This was India's second time hosting a global AI gathering after the AI Safety Summit lineage that began at Bletchley Park in the United Kingdom in November 2023, followed by Seoul in May 2024 and Paris in February 2025. New Delhi's rebrand from Safety to Impact signalled a shift in emphasis, from restricting AI's risks toward capturing its economic upside for the Global South, a framing India has pushed since it co-chaired the Global Partnership on AI.

The summit sits against a landscape a CLAT aspirant should hold in their head. OpenAI, founded in December 2015 as a non-profit by Sam Altman, Elon Musk and others, now competes with Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and China's DeepSeek, whose January 2025 model release rattled markets by showing frontier performance at a fraction of the training cost. The European Union's AI Act, which entered into force in August 2024, remains the world's most comprehensive binding AI law, classifying systems by risk tier from minimal to unacceptable. India itself has no standalone AI law; its principal instrument is the IndiaAI Mission, approved by the Cabinet in March 2024 with an outlay of over Rs 10,000 crore, covering compute infrastructure, datasets, and skilling.

For an exam, the trap is confusing the New Delhi Declaration, a voluntary multilateral statement with no binding force, for a treaty. It is closer in character to the G20 declarations India has hosted before, useful for signalling but not enforceable the way a WTO ruling or a UN Security Council resolution would be.

topics.title: US Supreme Court strikes down Trump's IEEPA tariffs
topics.hook: On February 20, 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled 6-3 that the President cannot impose tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, unwinding Donald Trump's signature trade policy.
topics.story:
The US Supreme Court decided Learning Resources Inc. v. Trump and the consolidated V.O.S. Selections v. United States on February 20, 2026, ruling 6-3 that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, or IEEPA, does not give the President authority to impose tariffs. The law, passed in 1977 to let presidents regulate transactions during declared national emergencies, had been the legal basis for Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs and his reciprocal tariff regime, which by February 2026 had raised more than $160 billion for the federal government and was projected to raise $1.4 trillion between 2026 and 2035 had it continued.

The Court's reasoning rested on the major questions doctrine and the constitutional text itself: Article I of the US Constitution gives Congress, not the President, the power to lay and collect taxes, and the majority held that IEEPA's language authorising the President to regulate importation does not stretch to include a power as consequential as tariff-setting. All tariffs imposed under IEEPA terminated at midnight Eastern time on February 24, 2026.

Trump did not accept defeat quietly. The same day the ruling came down, he signed a proclamation invoking Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, a narrower and time-limited authority, to impose a 10% global import surcharge, exempting goods that qualify as originating under the USMCA. Section 122 allows a president to impose a surcharge of up to 15% for no more than 150 days to address balance-of-payments problems, which is a far weaker tool than the open-ended IEEPA tariffs the Court had just voided.

The ruling landed only two weeks after India and the US had struck a trade framework, announced February 7, 2026, that set a reciprocal tariff rate of 18% on Indian exports and committed India to buying $500 billion worth of American energy products, aircraft, and metals by 2031. That framework, negotiated partly under the IEEPA authority the Court struck down, was thrown into legal uncertainty, though the Trump administration signalled it would try to preserve the substance of country-specific deals through other statutory routes such as Section 122 or Section 301 investigations.

For a CLAT aspirant, the comparative angle matters: India's own Constitution splits taxing power differently, with Article 265 providing that no tax can be levied or collected except by authority of law, and customs duties falling under the Union List via the Customs Act, 1962, itself passed by Parliament rather than imposed by executive proclamation. The American case is a live example of separation of powers doctrine, useful for any comparative constitutional law question that asks how different systems check executive overreach on money matters.

topics.title: Macron in Mumbai: India and France declare a 'Special Global Strategic Partnership'
topics.hook: President Emmanuel Macron's February 17-19 visit to India produced a 'Special Global Strategic Partnership', the highest tier France has offered any country, and launched the India-France Year of Innovation.
topics.story:
Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte arrived in India on February 17, 2026, his fourth visit since taking office in 2017. The centrepiece was a joint decision with Prime Minister Narendra Modi to upgrade the relationship to a 'Special Global Strategic Partnership', language chosen to sit above the existing Strategic Partnership that France and India signed back in January 1998, four months before India's Pokhran-II nuclear tests. France was, notably, one of the few major powers that did not condemn India over those tests, a diplomatic memory that still colours how Delhi frames the France relationship as more reliable than its ties with Washington or Moscow.

The two leaders inaugurated the India-France Year of Innovation 2026 in Mumbai on February 17, and agreed to institutionalise annual meetings between their foreign ministers to operationalise something called the Horizon 2047 Roadmap, a bilateral document mapping cooperation through the centenary of Indian independence. Macron also used the trip to join the AI Impact Summit running concurrently in New Delhi, giving France a visible seat at India's flagship 2026 diplomatic event.

Defence cooperation, already the backbone of the relationship since India bought 36 Rafale fighter jets from Dassault Aviation in a 2016 government-to-government deal, deepened further. Days before Macron's arrival, on February 12, the Defence Acquisition Council had cleared a Rs 3.6 lakh crore package that included further Rafale procurement and a joint venture between Hindustan Aeronautics Limited and the French firm Safran to produce HAMMER precision-guided munitions in India, tying the visit to a concrete manufacturing commitment rather than just a communique.

The timing traced back to January 2026, when External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar met Macron in Paris to discuss defence, space, civil nuclear energy, and maritime security, groundwork that set up the February state visit. France remains one of India's oldest civil nuclear partners, having signed a 2008 agreement enabling nuclear cooperation after the Nuclear Suppliers Group granted India a waiver that year, and the Jaitapur nuclear power project in Maharashtra, still under negotiation with the French firm EDF, was among the topics raised.

For an exam, this topic tests two things at once: recall of India's defence-supplier map, where France (Rafale, Scorpene submarines built under technology transfer at Mazagon Dock) sits alongside Russia and the United States, and the broader pattern of India's 'multi-alignment' foreign policy, in which it elevates partnerships with multiple powers simultaneously rather than choosing a single bloc.

topics.title: BNP sweeps Bangladesh's first election since the Hasina uprising
topics.hook: Bangladesh voted on February 12, 2026 in its first general election since the 2024 uprising, and Tarique Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party won 209 of 299 seats, ending 20 years out of power.
topics.story:
Bangladesh held its general election on February 12, 2026, the country's first national vote since the student-led uprising of July-August 2024 forced Sheikh Hasina, prime minister for a continuous 15 years, to flee to India. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party, led by Tarique Rahman, won a landslide, taking 209 of the 299 elected seats in the Jatiya Sangsad. Jamaat-e-Islami, contesting on its own rather than in the BNP-led coalitions of past elections, emerged as the largest opposition force with 68 seats, a sharp gain that reflects how the political map has been reshuffled since Hasina's Awami League was barred from contesting.

Tarique Rahman is the son of Ziaur Rahman, a former army chief who founded the BNP and served as President of Bangladesh from 1977 until his assassination in 1981, and of Khaleda Zia, herself a two-time prime minister and BNP chairperson who has been in and out of power since the 1990s. Tarique had lived in exile in London for years facing corruption charges under the Hasina government, charges his supporters called politically motivated, and his return to lead the BNP to victory closes a loop that began with his mother's rivalry against Hasina across the 1990s and 2000s, a period Bangladeshis call the 'Battle of the Begums'.

The Awami League's exclusion from this election followed its ban by the interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, who took over as Chief Adviser after Hasina's fall in August 2024 and oversaw the transition to this vote. Hasina herself remains outside Bangladesh; an International Crimes Tribunal in Dhaka convicted her in absentia in November 2025 for crimes against humanity connected to the crackdown on the 2024 protests, in which UN estimates put the death toll above 1,400.

Modi called Rahman to congratulate him on the win, a diplomatically necessary gesture given how central Bangladesh is to India's eastern neighbourhood, but also a delicate one: the BNP has historically been viewed in Delhi as less accommodating to Indian interests than the Awami League, and Bangladesh under the interim government had already seen friction with India, including over Hasina's continued presence on Indian soil.

For CLAT, the useful frame is neighbourhood-first diplomacy. Bangladesh is India's largest trading partner in South Asia, and the two share a land and river border longer than India shares with any other neighbour, including the Teesta water-sharing dispute that has stalled for over a decade and will now need fresh negotiation with a BNP government less familiar to Indian negotiators than the Awami League was.

topics.title: One month after Maduro's capture, Venezuela weighs an uncertain recovery
topics.hook: A month after a US military operation captured President Nicolas Maduro on January 3, 2026, CNN reported Venezuelans caught between eased sanctions and a wrecked economy, with acting president Delcy Rodriguez releasing political prisoners.
topics.story:
On January 3, 2026, the United States carried out a military strike in Venezuela and captured President Nicolas Maduro along with his wife, Cilia Flores, flying them to New York, where Maduro faces indictment on narcoterrorism and cocaine-trafficking conspiracy charges. By February 4, when CNN filed its one-month-later report from Caracas, the country remained suspended between the old order and an unclear new one: Vice President Delcy Rodriguez had stepped in as acting president and begun releasing political prisoners, a process that by early March had freed 621 people according to the Venezuelan NGO Foro Penal, with over 500 more still detained.

Maduro had ruled Venezuela since 2013, succeeding Hugo Chavez, who founded the self-styled Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, renamed from the Republic of Venezuela in 1999 in honour of Simon Bolivar, the 19th-century independence leader who liberated much of northern South America from Spanish rule and remains the region's most invoked political symbol. Chavez's government and Maduro's after him leaned on Bolivar's legacy to frame their socialist project as a continuation of anti-imperialist liberation, even as the US repeatedly accused both of authoritarianism and, more recently, of running a narco-state.

US justification for the operation traced back, rhetorically at least, to the Monroe Doctrine of 1823, announced by President James Monroe in his seventh annual message to Congress, which declared that European powers should not interfere in the Western Hemisphere and that the United States would treat such interference as a threat to its own peace and safety. The doctrine has been invoked, reinterpreted, and criticised for two centuries, from the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 that asserted a US right to intervene in Latin American states to enforce order, through Cold War interventions in Guatemala, Cuba, and Chile, to this 2026 operation, which the administration framed as a counter-narcotics and hemispheric-security action rather than territorial conquest.

Venezuela's economic weight complicates any simple reading. It holds the world's largest proven oil reserves and was a founding member of OPEC in 1960 alongside Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia, though years of US sanctions, first tightened sharply in 2019, and mismanagement had already cut its oil output far below capacity before Maduro's capture. As sanctions eased in early 2026, oil money began trickling back, but ordinary wages, CNN reported, still barely covered food.

Regional reaction split along familiar lines: the Organization of American States, the hemispheric body founded in 1948 and headquartered in Washington, saw member states divided between those welcoming Maduro's removal and those, including some left-leaning governments, condemning the operation as a violation of sovereignty reminiscent of earlier US interventions the OAS itself has been accused of enabling.

topics.title: Milano Cortina 2026: two Italian cities share the Winter Olympics
topics.hook: The Olympic Winter Games opened February 6, 2026 in Milan and Cortina d'Ampezzo, the first Winter Olympics officially hosted by two cities, running through February 22.
topics.story:
The XXV Olympic Winter Games ran from February 6 to 22, 2026, split between Milan and the alpine resort town of Cortina d'Ampezzo, roughly 400 kilometres apart, making this the first Winter Olympics with two official host cities rather than one. Around 2,800 athletes competed across 16 sport disciplines and 116 events, including ski mountaineering, added to the Winter programme for the first time. Cortina had hosted the Winter Games once before, in 1956, the first Winter Olympics broadcast on television, which gives Italy the distinction of hosting the Winter Games across three different decades, joining a short list of repeat Winter hosts that includes the United States, France, and Japan.

Competitions technically began on February 4, two days before the Opening Ceremony on February 6, a scheduling quirk the IOC has used before to accommodate events like curling mixed doubles that need extra match days. The Closing Ceremony fell on February 22. A separate Paralympic Winter Games followed at the same venues from March 6 to 15, 2026, organised by the International Paralympic Committee, a distinct body from the International Olympic Committee though the two now coordinate host-city bids jointly.

The IOC itself, founded in 1894 by Pierre de Coubertin in Paris, is headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, and the first modern Olympics it organised were held in Athens in 1896. The Winter Games are a comparatively young tradition, first held in Chamonix, France in 1924, initially just called 'International Winter Sports Week' before being retroactively recognised as the first Winter Olympics.

For India, Winter Olympics coverage in a general-knowledge exam usually tests peripheral facts: India has historically sent small contingents to the Winter Games, its best individual result remaining Shiva Keshavan's appearances in luge across six consecutive Games from 1998 to 2018, and India has never won a Winter Olympic medal. The more testable material tends to be about the host structure and organisational trivia: the IOC's session-based selection of host cities, the environmental and cost controversies that made cities like Stockholm and Sion withdraw their bids for 2026 before Milan-Cortina was awarded the Games in 2019, and the growing pattern of co-hosting arrangements as a response to the ballooning cost of building single-city Winter Olympic infrastructure.

topics.title: Parliament passes the Industrial Relations Code (Amendment) Bill, closing out the labour codes rollout
topics.hook: Both Houses passed the Industrial Relations Code (Amendment) Bill, 2026 during the February leg of the Budget Session, confirming that three old labour laws stood repealed from November 21, 2025.
topics.story:
Introduced and passed by both Houses on February 11, 2026, the Industrial Relations Code (Amendment) Bill clarified that three predecessor statutes, the Trade Unions Act of 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act of 1946, and the Industrial Disputes Act of 1947, stood formally repealed as of November 21, 2025, the date the four consolidated labour codes came into force. The bill was one of nine bills Parliament passed during the Budget Session's February leg, before both Houses adjourned for recess on February 13 and reassembled on March 9.

The four labour codes, the Code on Wages (2019), the Industrial Relations Code (2020), the Code on Social Security (2020), and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (2020), together replace 29 separate central labour statutes accumulated since colonial times, an exercise the government frames as ease-of-compliance reform and unions have long criticised as diluting worker protections, particularly the higher threshold set for 'standing orders' and layoff permissions in larger firms. Detailed implementation rules for the Code on Wages, Code on Social Security, and the Occupational Safety Code were still under a public comment window running to February 14, 2026, meaning that even as the codes were formally in force, the fine print governing their day-to-day application was still being finalised through February.

The Industrial Relations Code, the specific subject of this amendment, governs trade union recognition, the machinery for resolving industrial disputes, and the conditions under which employers can lay off or retrench workers. Its provisions interact directly with a long-running constitutional question the Supreme Court was simultaneously revisiting: what does 'industry' mean under Section 2(j) of the old Industrial Disputes Act, a definition so contested that the Court has referred it to a nine-judge Constitution Bench, revived mid-February 2026 after years of dormancy.

Sector-wise, banking and IT/ITeS firms had already started reporting the codes' impact on their December-quarter profits by the time this amendment passed, largely through changed provident fund and gratuity calculation methods under the Code on Social Security, which redefines 'wages' more broadly to include allowances previously excluded, pushing up employer contribution costs.

For CLAT, labour law rarely gets a full passage to itself but shows up as a polity or economy sub-question: know that labour falls in the Concurrent List (List III) of the Seventh Schedule, meaning both Parliament and state legislatures can legislate on it, which is why several states have sought their own implementation timelines for the codes even after the central law came into force.

topics.title: Modi's Israel visit elevates ties to a 'Special Strategic Partnership'
topics.hook: Prime Minister Modi's February 25-26 state visit to Israel produced a 'Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity' and 16 agreements spanning AI, agriculture, and defence.
topics.story:
Narendra Modi travelled to Israel on a two-day state visit, February 25-26, 2026, meeting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem to elevate bilateral relations to a 'Special Strategic Partnership for Peace, Innovation and Prosperity,' the highest diplomatic tier the two countries have used for each other. The two sides signed 16 agreements covering artificial intelligence, critical minerals, defence and security cooperation, trade, labour mobility, education, the blue economy, agriculture, and health.

India and Israel established full diplomatic relations only in January 1992, a notably late date given how long both countries had existed by then, a gap that traces back to India's Cold War-era non-alignment and its outreach to the Arab world, particularly its vocal support for Palestinian statehood, which it maintained even as it quietly bought Israeli military equipment through back channels for decades before formal ties opened. Since 1992, the relationship has grown mostly through defence: Israel is among India's top arms suppliers, providing missile defence systems, drones, and surveillance technology, and cooperation deepened sharply after Modi became the first Indian Prime Minister to visit Israel, in July 2017, a visit notable partly for what it omitted, a stop in Ramallah, breaking with the earlier practice of pairing Israel visits with a symbolic Palestine visit.

Agriculture has been a quieter but longer thread: Israel's drip-irrigation and precision-farming technology, developed to farm in a water-scarce desert environment, has been transferred to Indian states through Centres of Excellence set up under bilateral agreements dating to 2006, well before the 2017 political upgrade.

The February 2026 visit landed against the backdrop of the Gaza ceasefire that began October 10, 2025, one still marked by continuing violence, so the trip carried a diplomatic cost calculation: India has historically tried to balance support for Israel with its relationships across the Gulf and its traditional position favouring a two-state solution, a position it has not formally abandoned even as ties with Israel deepen. India abstained on several UN General Assembly resolutions concerning Gaza through late 2025 and early 2026 rather than voting squarely with either bloc, illustrating this balancing act in practice.

For an exam, the useful anchor points are the 1992 date for full diplomatic relations, the 2017 visit as the first by a sitting Indian PM, and India's continued formal support for a two-state solution even as the practical relationship, especially in defence and technology, has become one of India's closest.

topics.title: Supreme Court finally takes up the CAA's constitutional challenge
topics.hook: Nearly two years after petitions were filed, the Supreme Court on February 19, 2026 began substantive hearings on the constitutionality of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, starting with pan-India objections before turning to Assam and Tripura-specific claims.
topics.story:
The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, passed by Parliament in December 2019, fast-tracks Indian citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian migrants who entered India from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan before December 31, 2014, while excluding Muslims from the same fast-track route. It triggered nationwide protests through late 2019 and early 2020, most visibly the Shaheen Bagh sit-in in Delhi, and more than 200 petitions challenging its validity piled up before the Supreme Court, largely on the ground that excluding Muslims specifically, rather than all undocumented migrants regardless of religion, violates Article 14's guarantee of equality before the law.

The Act itself was not implemented for years after passage; the Rules needed to operationalise it were notified only in March 2024, just before the general election, prompting further litigation over the timing. On February 19, 2026, the Court finally began substantive hearings, directing that pan-India concerns about the law's constitutionality be argued first, with the geographically specific challenges from Assam and Tripura, states with their own particular anxieties about demographic change from cross-border migration, to be taken up afterward.

Assam's objection is distinct and older: the state's political mainstream, going back to the Assam Movement of 1979-85, has long opposed granting citizenship to any migrants who arrived after March 24, 1971, the cutoff date fixed by the Assam Accord of 1985 and written into Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955. The CAA's cutoff of December 31, 2014, is thirteen years later than the Assam Accord's cutoff, which is precisely why Assamese groups argue the CAA effectively overrides a negotiated settlement that ended a six-year agitation.

The case sits alongside the National Register of Citizens exercise, last updated for Assam in 2019 under Supreme Court supervision, which excluded over 19 lakh applicants and remains contested and largely unimplemented years later, a separate but conceptually linked question about who counts as a citizen and how proof is established. Constitutionally, both CAA and NRC questions eventually return to Article 11, which gives Parliament the power to regulate citizenship by law, a power exercised through the Citizenship Act, 1955, of which the CAA is the sixth substantial amendment.

For CLAT, the exam-relevant distinction is between the CAA (a route to citizenship, adding categories of eligible migrants) and the NRC (a verification exercise determining who is already a citizen); students routinely conflate the two, and a well-built distractor question will exploit exactly that confusion.

topics.title: India and China keep managing a cautious border thaw
topics.hook: Building on Wang Yi's 2025 visit, India and China moved through February 2026 to set up a general-level talks mechanism on their disputed boundary, even as Jaishankar insisted peace at the border remains a precondition for normal ties.
topics.story:
China and India spent early 2026 consolidating a diplomatic thaw that began after the 2020 Galwan Valley clash, the deadliest border confrontation between the two since 1967, which killed 20 Indian soldiers and an unconfirmed number of Chinese troops and froze high-level engagement for years afterward. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's visit to New Delhi, where he met National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Prime Minister Modi, had already produced an agreement to establish a general-level talks mechanism covering the eastern and central sectors of the Line of Actual Control, building on the Special Representatives dialogue that Doval has run opposite Wang Yi since 2003.

Both countries agreed to support each other's hosting of major diplomatic events in 2026, with China backing India's turn to host the BRICS summit, the grouping originally formed as BRIC in 2009 by Brazil, Russia, India, and China, joined by South Africa in 2010 and expanded further in 2024 to include Iran, the UAE, Egypt, and Ethiopia among others. Jaishankar, in his public remarks through this period, repeatedly returned to a consistent formulation: that peace and tranquillity at the border is a prerequisite, not a byproduct, of normalised relations, a phrasing meant to resist any Chinese framing that economic and diplomatic normalisation could proceed independently of a durable border settlement.

The unresolved core remains the 3,488-kilometre Line of Actual Control, not a formally demarcated international border but a loosely defined line of military control established after the 1962 Sino-Indian War, which India lost badly in the eastern and western sectors. Disengagement processes at friction points like Depsang and Demchok, agreed upon in October 2024 after the Kazan BRICS summit meeting between Modi and Xi Jinping, continued into 2026, though de-escalation, meaning troop reduction, remains a separate and unfinished step beyond disengagement, which only means troops pulling back from face-to-face contact points.

For an exam, the useful distinctions are these: LAC is not the same as the McMahon Line, which specifically demarcates the eastern sector boundary that China has never accepted, drawn at the 1914 Simla Convention between British India and Tibet; and 'disengagement' at friction points is a narrower, more limited step than full 'de-escalation' of troop presence along the frontier, a distinction examiners like to test with a fact-check option.

topics.title: India Semiconductor Mission 2.0: from policy to fabrication
topics.hook: The Budget cleared India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 at an overall outlay of Rs 1.25 lakh crore, up from Rs 76,000 crore for the first phase, shifting focus from capacity creation to deeper fabrication and design.
topics.story:
India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 received Expenditure Finance Committee clearance ahead of the February 1 Budget, with an overall proposed outlay of Rs 1.25 lakh crore, or roughly $13.21 billion, against Rs 76,000 crore, about $8.03 billion, allocated to the original mission launched in December 2021. The Budget itself carried a direct FY27 provision of Rs 1,000 crore for ISM 2.0, alongside Rs 8,000 crore for the related Modified Programme for Development of Semiconductor and Display Manufacturing Ecosystem, the scheme that actually disburses capital subsidies to chip fabrication plants.

The first phase of the mission had already produced its early wins by 2026: the Micron Technology assembly and test facility in Sanand, Gujarat, announced in 2023, and India's first commercial semiconductor fabrication plant, also planned for Gujarat by the Tata Group in partnership with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation. ISM 2.0 is meant to move the country from these initial assembly-and-test operations toward genuine fabrication depth, including support for producing the specialised equipment, chemicals, and gases a chip fab needs, categories India currently imports almost entirely.

Two sub-programmes anchor the new phase. The Design Linked Incentive Scheme supports fabless companies, the term for firms that design chips but outsource manufacturing to specialised foundries such as Taiwan's TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker and the manufacturer behind most of Apple and Nvidia's most advanced processors. The Digital India RISC-V Programme backs an open-source chip architecture that carries no licensing fees, unlike the dominant proprietary architectures from ARM Holdings and Intel's x86, giving Indian startups and universities a lower-cost entry point into chip design.

Globally, the semiconductor supply chain remains concentrated in ways India's mission is explicitly trying to diversify: the Netherlands' ASML holds a near-monopoly on the extreme ultraviolet lithography machines needed for the most advanced chips, and Taiwan alone produces the overwhelming majority of the world's most advanced sub-7-nanometre chips through TSMC, a concentration that became a strategic anxiety for governments worldwide after COVID-era chip shortages stalled car and electronics production in 2021-22.

This is also the context for the Pax Silica Coalition, which India joined on February 20, 2026, alongside Australia, Israel, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, the UAE, the UK, and the US, explicitly aimed at securing semiconductor and critical mineral supply chains against overreliance on any single geography, an unmistakable reference to Taiwan's outsized role and to China's dominance in rare-earth processing.

topics.title: Economic Survey 2025-26 and a rebased GDP series
topics.hook: Tabled a day before the Budget, the Economic Survey projected 7.4% growth for FY26, while a newly rebased GDP series with 2022-23 as the base year showed manufacturing growing fastest at 11.5%.
topics.story:
The Chief Economic Adviser tabled the Economic Survey 2025-26 on January 29, 2026, projecting real GDP growth of 7.4% for the current financial year and a range of 6.8% to 7.2% for 2026-27, framed as continued proof that India remains the fastest-growing major economy even as global trade faced disruption from the US tariff fights running through February. The Survey flagged multi-decade lows in bank non-performing assets, with the gross NPA ratio at 2.2%, and pointed to cumulative repo rate cuts of 125 basis points since February 2025 as evidence that monetary easing was finally reaching borrowers.

Separately, in February, the government released a rebased GDP series shifting the base year to 2022-23 from the earlier 2011-12 base, a periodic statistical exercise the Central Statistics Office undertakes to keep national accounts reflecting the current structure of the economy, including sectors like digital services that barely existed when the last base year was fixed. Under the new series, FY26 growth was estimated at 7.6% at constant prices, with manufacturing the fastest-growing sector at 11.5%, ahead of trade at 10.1%.

Rebasing exercises change the reported growth rate without changing the underlying economy, a distinction CLAT examiners like to probe: a higher reported growth number after rebasing does not mean the economy suddenly grew faster, only that the measurement yardstick shifted. India's GDP base year has moved several times, from 1993-94 to 1999-2000 to 2004-05 to 2011-12, and now to 2022-23, each revision drawing some criticism over methodology, most notably after the 2011-12 rebasing in 2015 was challenged by economists including former CEA Arvind Subramanian for allegedly overstating growth.

External indicators cited in the Survey rounded out the picture: remittances at $135.4 billion and forex reserves at $701.4 billion, both cushioning India's external position against the kind of currency pressure that has hit countries with thinner reserves.
topics.why: A likely trap question asks whether rebasing GDP changes the real economy; the correct answer is no, it only changes the measurement base. Expect the base-year sequence (1993-94 to 2022-23) tested as a standalone fact.

topics.title: RBI holds the repo rate at 5.25% for a second straight meeting
topics.hook: The Monetary Policy Committee, meeting February 4-6, 2026, unanimously kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%, with Governor Sanjay Malhotra citing benign inflation and resilient growth.
topics.story:
The Reserve Bank of India's six-member Monetary Policy Committee met February 4-6, 2026, and voted unanimously to hold the repo rate, the rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks, at 5.25%, unchanged for a second consecutive bi-monthly meeting. The standing deposit facility rate stayed at 5%, and the marginal standing facility rate at 5.5%, both moving in lockstep with the repo rate as they are designed to.

Governor Sanjay Malhotra, who took charge of the RBI in December 2024, maintained the committee's 'neutral' policy stance, meaning future moves could go either way depending on incoming data, rather than a committed easing or tightening bias. He pointed to headline inflation running below the RBI's upper tolerance band and projected CPI inflation of 4% for the first quarter of FY27 and 4.2% for the second quarter, both comfortably within the RBI's medium-term target of 4%, with a tolerance band of plus or minus 2 percentage points, set under the flexible inflation targeting framework adopted in 2016.

The MPC itself was created by an amendment to the RBI Act, 1934, following the 2016 monetary policy framework agreement between the government and the RBI; it has six members, three from the RBI including the Governor, who holds a casting vote in case of a tie, and three external members appointed by the central government. Since the RBI cut rates cumulatively by 125 basis points through 2025, the February pause signalled the easing cycle had likely run its course for the moment, with the central bank now watching how previous cuts filter through to actual bank lending rates before moving further.

topics.title: Gaza's ceasefire holds on paper as strikes continue
topics.hook: Despite a ceasefire in place since October 10, 2025, Israeli strikes killed at least 23 Palestinians in Gaza on February 4, 2026 alone, part of a pattern of continued violence through the month.
topics.story:
The Gaza ceasefire that took effect on October 10, 2025 was still formally in force through February 2026, but the month's record showed how porous that peace remained. Israeli strikes on February 4 killed at least 23 Palestinians, many of them children, and Al Jazeera characterised the pattern as 'shattering the ceasefire myth.' Since the ceasefire began, at least 618 Palestinians in Gaza had been killed in Israeli attacks by early February, according to figures cited from Gaza's Civil Defence, alongside separate violence in the occupied West Bank that killed five Palestinians during the month, including a child and a US citizen, at the hands of Israeli forces and settlers.

On the humanitarian side, Israel transferred 54 bodies and 66 boxes of remains of Palestinians to Gaza authorities on February 4, while Civil Defence teams reported documenting nearly 3,000 people whose bodies had been effectively vaporised in earlier Israeli strikes using US-supplied thermal and thermobaric munitions. Aid flows continued unevenly: over 283,000 pallets of humanitarian cargo had been offloaded into Gaza between the ceasefire's start and early February, even as more than 18,500 patients, including 4,000 children, still needed specialised medical care unavailable inside the Strip.

The ceasefire itself followed roughly two years of war that began after Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, and was brokered with US, Qatari, and Egyptian mediation, echoing the structure of the earlier November 2023 truce that had also involved hostage-prisoner exchanges. For CLAT, the useful frame is that a 'ceasefire' is a negotiated pause in hostilities, not a peace treaty ending the underlying conflict, a distinction that explains why violations can continue even while the ceasefire formally holds.

topics.title: India and the US strike an 18% tariff trade framework, then watch it wobble
topics.hook: India and the United States announced a trade framework on February 7, 2026 setting an 18% reciprocal tariff on Indian exports, only for the US Supreme Court to void its legal basis two weeks later.
topics.story:
On February 7, 2026, India and the United States announced a trade framework setting a reciprocal tariff rate of 18% on Indian exports to the US, alongside an Indian commitment to purchase $500 billion worth of American energy products, aircraft, and metals by 2031. The deal was meant to settle months of tariff friction that had seen Indian goods hit with rates as high as 50% earlier in the Trump administration's tenure over India's continued purchase of Russian oil, one of the sharpest trade disputes in the relationship's recent history.

The framework's legal foundation cracked almost immediately: on February 20, 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the law underlying Trump's reciprocal tariff programme worldwide, did not authorise tariffs at all, voiding the executive orders the India deal had been built on. Trump's administration pivoted to Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, a narrower 150-day authority, to keep some tariff pressure in place while it worked out how to preserve country-specific arrangements like the one with India through other legal routes.

For India, the trade relationship carries weight beyond any single tariff number: the US has been India's largest trading partner for goods since overtaking China around 2021-22, and IT services exports to US clients form a large share of India's software industry revenue, making tariff and visa policy toward India-based firms and their US-bound engineers, the H-1B visa programme among them, a recurring friction point independent of goods tariffs.

topics.title: India joins the Pax Silica Coalition on chip supply chains
topics.hook: India joined the newly formed Pax Silica Coalition on February 20, 2026, alongside Australia, Israel, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, the UAE, the UK, and the US, to secure semiconductor and critical mineral supply chains.
topics.story:
Announced February 20, 2026, the Pax Silica Coalition brought together nine countries, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, the UAE, the UK, and the United States, around a shared goal of insulating semiconductor and critical mineral supply chains from concentration in any single geography. The name echoes 'Pax Silicon Valley' style framing common in tech-geopolitics writing, silica being the raw material refined into the silicon wafers chips are built on.

The coalition responds to two concentration risks specialists flag repeatedly: Taiwan's TSMC fabricates the overwhelming majority of the world's most advanced chips, making the island a single point of failure that would be catastrophic if disrupted by conflict, and China controls an outsized share of global rare-earth element processing, elements essential not just for chips but for electric vehicle motors, wind turbines, and precision-guided weapons. China has periodically restricted rare-earth exports as diplomatic leverage, most notably during trade disputes with Japan in 2010 and again amid the broader US-China tech rivalry through the 2020s.

For India, joining signals an attempt to be positioned as an alternative node in this supply chain, dovetailing with the Semiconductor Mission 2.0 outlay announced in the same Budget cycle, and with India's own push, through the Ministry of Mines' 2023 Critical Minerals push, to secure lithium, cobalt, and rare-earth supplies both domestically and through overseas mining partnerships in countries like Argentina and Australia.

India and the Gulf Cooperation Council signed terms of reference on February 5, 2026, the formal document that sets the scope, structure, and ground rules for free trade agreement negotiations before substantive talks begin. The GCC, formed in 1981 and comprising Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, and Oman, is collectively India's largest trading bloc partner in the Gulf, with two-way trade worth $179 billion in 2024-25, driven heavily by India's crude oil imports and its remittance-heavy expatriate workforce, which numbers in the millions across the six member states.

India already has separate bilateral trade agreements with individual GCC members, most notably the India-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement signed in 2022, one of India's fastest-negotiated trade deals. topics.title: Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 gets a Rs 10,000 crore corpus
topics.hook: The Cabinet approved Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 on February 14, 2026 with a Rs 10,000 crore corpus, targeting high-tech, early-stage, and non-metro founders.
topics.story:
The Union Cabinet cleared Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 on February 14, 2026, with a corpus of Rs 10,000 crore aimed squarely at high-tech sectors, early-stage founders, and non-metro investment, a deliberate push to spread venture capital beyond the Bengaluru-Delhi-Mumbai concentration that has dominated Indian startup funding since the sector took off in the 2010s.

A 'Fund of Funds' does not invest directly in startups; instead, it invests in venture capital funds, which then invest in individual companies, a structure meant to leverage government money several times over by crowding in private capital rather than picking winners directly. The original Fund of Funds for Startups, launched in 2016 under the Startup India initiative with a Rs 10,000 crore corpus managed by SIDBI, the Small Industries Development Bank of India, is credited with having backed hundreds of funds that in turn supported thousands of startups, including some that later became unicorns, companies valued above $1 billion.

The 2.0 version arrives as India's unicorn count, once growing rapidly through 2021-22, cooled through the following years amid a global venture capital funding slowdown, giving the scheme's non-metro and deep-tech focus added significance as an attempt to diversify beyond the consumer internet startups that dominated the first wave.

Chaired by the Defence Minister, the Defence Acquisition Council cleared procurement worth Rs 3.6 lakh crore on February 12, 2026, the apex approval body that vets major capital defence purchases before they move to contract negotiation and, eventually, Cabinet Committee on Security sign-off for the largest deals. The cleared package spanned further Rafale fighter procurement from France's Dassault Aviation, upgrades to the Soviet-origin T-72 tank fleet that still forms a substantial share of India's armoured strength, additional P-8I Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft built by Boeing for long-range submarine hunting and maritime surveillance, and a joint venture between Hindustan Aeronautics Limited and France's Safran to manufacture HAMMER precision-guided munitions domestically.

The clearance landed five days before President Macron's state visit, timing that let both governments point to a concrete manufacturing commitment rather than just a diplomatic communique when they met in Mumbai. The DAC framework itself operates through categories such as 'Buy Indian', 'Buy and Make Indian', and 'Buy Global', a hierarchy the Defence Ministry has increasingly tilted toward domestic categories since the Atmanirbhar Bharat, or self-reliant India, push accelerated after 2020, though platforms like the P-8I and further Rafale units still require foreign sourcing where India lacks comparable indigenous capability.

topics.title: West Bengal's electoral roll revision reaches the Supreme Court
topics.hook: With 1.36 crore West Bengal voters flagged in questionable categories and 32 lakh unmapped, the Supreme Court extended deadlines and authorised Additional District Judges to hear claims before final rolls were published on February 28, 2026.
topics.story:
The Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, of West Bengal's electoral rolls became a live Supreme Court matter in February 2026 after the Election Commission's exercise flagged 1.36 crore voters in questionable categories, meaning entries needing further verification, and left 32 lakh voters unmapped to any polling booth, numbers large enough in a state with roughly 7 crore registered voters to threaten the credibility of any election held on the resulting rolls. The Court extended the claims-and-objections deadline and, unusually, authorised Additional District Judges to adjudicate contested entries alongside the normal Electoral Registration Officer machinery, a move meant to clear the backlog before West Bengal's assembly election, due in 2026.

Final rolls were published on February 28, 2026, closing this phase of the exercise, though the political controversy around SIR did not end there. The Trinamool Congress, West Bengal's ruling party, had accused the Election Commission of using the revision to disenfranchise migrant and minority voters, an echo of similar objections raised earlier when SIR was first rolled out in Bihar. The Election Commission, a constitutional body under Article 324, is empowered to superintend, direct, and control elections, and periodic roll revisions are a routine statutory exercise under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, but the scale of flagged entries in West Bengal made this round unusually contentious.

topics.title: Supreme Court revives a 9-judge bench to define 'industry'
topics.hook: On February 16, 2026, the Supreme Court revived a long-dormant reference to a nine-judge Constitution Bench to settle what counts as an 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
topics.story:
The Supreme Court on February 16, 2026 revived two nine-judge bench references, dormant for years, to finally resolve the definition of 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a provision whose scope determines which workplaces, hospitals, universities, charitable trusts, and government departments among them, fall under labour law protections for workers. The seven-judge bench decision in Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa, decided in 1978, had given 'industry' an expansive reading covering almost any organised activity involving cooperation between employer and employee to produce goods or services, a reading later criticised as too broad and referred to a larger bench for reconsideration, a reference that then sat unresolved for decades.

The question has fresh urgency now because the Industrial Disputes Act itself stood repealed from November 21, 2025 as the four labour codes took effect, yet the Industrial Relations Code, 2020 that replaces it carries forward a similarly broad definition, meaning the Court's eventual ruling on 'industry' will still shape how the new code applies to hospitals, educational institutions, and religious or charitable bodies going forward.

The Summit traces back to 2001, when it began as the Delhi Sustainable Development Summit, positioning itself early as a Global South platform centring climate justice and equity rather than following the agenda set by wealthier, historically higher-emitting nations at forums like the UN Climate Change Conference, or COP, series.

Union Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav inaugurated the event and also launched the MoEFCC's Him-CONNECT platform, an initiative focused on Himalayan ecosystem monitoring and connectivity, at the same venue. TERI itself was founded in 1974 and is headed by Director General Vibha Dhawan; the institute is best known internationally for its long association with Rajendra Pachauri, who chaired the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change when it jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore in 2007, before Pachauri's tenure at both TERI and the IPCC ended amid a 2015 scandal.

topics.title: State of India's Environment 2026 warns seven planetary boundaries are breached
topics.hook: Released at the Anil Agarwal Dialogue on February 25, 2026, the Centre for Science and Environment's annual report found extreme weather struck India on 99% of days in 2025 and that seven of nine planetary boundaries have now been breached.
topics.story:
The Centre for Science and Environment and its publication Down To Earth released the State of India's Environment 2026 report at the Anil Agarwal Dialogue on February 25, 2026, naming the event after the CSE's founder-director, who built the organisation into India's most prominent environmental advocacy body before his death in 2002. The report's headline finding: data from January 1 to November 30, 2025 showed extreme weather events, heatwaves, cold waves, heavy rainfall, and floods, striking India on 99% of days, killing 4,419 people and affecting 17.41 million hectares of crop area, the worst such year in the preceding four.

Globally, the report flagged that seven of nine recognised planetary boundaries, thresholds scientists use to define a 'safe operating space' for humanity across systems like climate, biosphere integrity, and freshwater, have now been breached, with ocean acidification the newest addition to that list. On air quality, the report noted a stark monitoring gap: only 15% of India's population lives within 10 kilometres of an air-quality monitoring station, leaving the remaining 85%, concentrated in smaller towns and industrial belts, essentially invisible to pollution data.

India beat England by 100 runs in the final of the Under-19 Cricket World Cup, played in Harare, Zimbabwe on February 7, 2026, taking the title for a record sixth time, more than any other country in the tournament's history. India's six titles, more than double any other nation's tally, reflect both the depth of India's domestic age-group cricket structure and the scouting reach of the Board of Control for Cricket in India, which runs the selection pipeline that increasingly feeds directly into the Indian Premier League auction pool for uncapped young players.
