passages.title: Reading the Budget beyond the headline number
passages.passage:
When Nirmala Sitharaman rose in the Lok Sabha on February 1, 2026 to deliver her ninth consecutive Budget speech, the number reporters chased hardest was the fiscal deficit target: 4.3% of GDP, trimmed from 4.4% the year before. But a Budget is not one number. It is the Annual Financial Statement that Article 112 of the Constitution requires the government to lay before Parliament each year, listing estimated receipts and expenditure for the coming financial year. Total expenditure for 2026-27 was pegged at Rs 53,47,315 crore, a 7.7% rise, while capital expenditure, the portion spent building roads, ports, and other assets rather than paying salaries or subsidies, rose to Rs 12.2 lakh crore.

The distinction between capital and revenue expenditure matters because economists treat them differently: capital spending is expected to crowd in private investment and lift future growth, while revenue spending is consumed in the year it is spent. The government's preference for capital expenditure over the past several Budgets reflects a bet that infrastructure spending compounds, even if it means slower progress on the fiscal deficit than a revenue-cutting approach might achieve.

No money leaves the government's coffers on the strength of a speech alone. Article 266 establishes the Consolidated Fund of India, and no withdrawal from it is lawful except through an Appropriation Act passed by Parliament. This is why the Finance Bill and Appropriation Bill that follow the Budget speech carry as much legal weight as the speech itself, even though they draw far less media attention. The Economic Survey, tabled a day before the Budget by the Chief Economic Adviser, projected 7.4% growth for the current year, a figure Sitharaman leaned on to argue India remained the world's fastest-growing large economy even as trade friction with the United States intensified through the month. Reading a Budget purely for its deficit number, in other words, misses most of what a Budget actually does.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The fiscal deficit target of 4.3% is the single most important figure in the Budget
A Budget is a constitutionally mandated document with legal machinery beyond its headline numbers
Capital expenditure is always superior to revenue expenditure
The Economic Survey is more important than the Budget speech
questions.explain: The passage's throughline is that reducing the Budget to one number, the fiscal deficit, misses its constitutional structure and legal mechanics. Option A isolates a detail the passage explicitly argues against treating as central; C and D overstate claims the passage doesn't make.

questions.q: According to the passage, why does the government prefer capital expenditure over revenue expenditure as a growth strategy?
options: Capital expenditure is easier to authorise under Article 112
Capital expenditure is expected to crowd in private investment and have compounding effects on growth
Revenue expenditure is unconstitutional under Article 266
Capital expenditure automatically reduces the fiscal deficit
questions.explain: The passage states capital spending is 'expected to crowd in private investment and lift future growth' because it builds assets, unlike revenue spending which is consumed immediately. The other options either invent a rule not in the passage or misstate the relationship.

questions.q: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage about the Finance Bill and Appropriation Bill?
options: They are ceremonial documents with no real legal effect
They carry legal weight because no money can leave the Consolidated Fund without them
They replace the need for a Budget speech altogether
They are passed before the Budget speech is delivered
questions.explain: The passage explicitly says these bills 'carry as much legal weight as the speech itself' because Article 266 bars withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund except through an Appropriation Act. They follow, not precede, the speech, ruling out D.

questions.q: Which statement about the Budget is true according to the passage?
options: The fiscal deficit target for 2026-27 was raised from the previous year
Total expenditure for 2026-27 was projected to fall compared to the previous year
The Economic Survey was tabled the day before the Budget by the Chief Economic Adviser
Capital expenditure declined to Rs 12.2 lakh crore
questions.explain: The passage states the Survey was tabled 'a day before the Budget by the Chief Economic Adviser.' The deficit target was cut, not raised (ruling out A); total expenditure rose 7.7% (ruling out B); and capital expenditure rose to, not fell to, Rs 12.2 lakh crore (ruling out D).

questions.q: The passage does not explain the difference between the Consolidated Fund of India and the Contingency Fund of India. Based on outside constitutional knowledge, which article establishes the Contingency Fund?
options: Article 112
Article 267
Article 280
Article 300
questions.explain: Article 267 establishes the Contingency Fund of India, used for unforeseen expenditure pending parliamentary authorisation, distinct from Article 266's Consolidated Fund and Article 112's Annual Financial Statement. This tests static constitutional knowledge the passage only gestures at.

passages.title: A single ruling, two countries' trade policy
passages.passage:
On February 20, 2026, the US Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Learning Resources Inc. v. Trump that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not authorise the President to impose tariffs, striking down the legal foundation of Donald Trump's global tariff programme. The reasoning drew on the plainest possible reading of the US Constitution: Article I gives Congress, not the President, the power to lay and collect taxes and duties, and the Court held that tariff-setting is exactly that kind of power, one too consequential to assume Congress meant to hand over through a 1977 law about regulating emergency transactions.

The ruling's reach extended well beyond American shores. Just two weeks earlier, on February 7, India and the United States had announced a trade framework built partly on IEEPA authority, setting a reciprocal tariff of 18% on Indian exports in exchange for India's commitment to buy $500 billion of American energy, aircraft, and metals by 2031. When the Court voided IEEPA's tariff power, it threw that framework's legal footing into question, forcing the Trump administration to scramble for an alternative. It found one in Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, a narrower authority letting a president impose a surcharge of up to 15% for no more than 150 days to address balance-of-payments problems, a temporary patch rather than the open-ended tool IEEPA had offered.

The episode is a live illustration of separation of powers doctrine, more vivid than any textbook hypothetical, because a court's domestic ruling on one country's constitutional structure rippled instantly into a bilateral trade arrangement thousands of miles away. It also offers an implicit comparison: India's own Constitution, through Article 265, similarly reserves taxing power to law rather than executive fiat, with the Customs Act, 1962 supplying the actual statutory basis Parliament, not the executive, must legislate.

questions.q: What is the central argument of the passage?
options: IEEPA is a well-designed law that the Supreme Court misapplied
A domestic constitutional ruling on separation of powers had immediate consequences for an international trade arrangement
India's Constitution is superior to the American Constitution on taxing power
Section 122 is a permanent replacement for IEEPA tariffs
questions.explain: The passage's core claim is that the ruling 'rippled instantly into a bilateral trade arrangement thousands of miles away,' making it a live illustration of how domestic constitutional law can have international consequences. Option D is wrong because the passage describes Section 122 as 'a temporary patch,' not permanent.

questions.q: Based on the passage, why did the Supreme Court rule against the IEEPA-based tariffs?
options: IEEPA explicitly prohibits tariffs in its text
The tariffs were racially discriminatory
Tariff-setting is a taxing power the Constitution reserves to Congress, not the President
The tariffs violated a WTO ruling
questions.explain: The passage states Article I 'gives Congress, not the President, the power to lay and collect taxes and duties' and the Court held tariffs fall within that category. The passage does not claim IEEPA explicitly bans tariffs, nor does it mention race or the WTO.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the India-US trade framework's status immediately after February 20, 2026?
options: It was automatically and permanently cancelled with no recourse
Its legal basis was undermined, prompting the US to seek an alternative statutory authority
It was unaffected because it involved India, not a US domestic matter
It was replaced immediately by a WTO-brokered agreement
questions.explain: The passage says the ruling 'threw that framework's legal footing into question, forcing the Trump administration to scramble for an alternative,' which it found in Section 122. It does not say the deal was cancelled outright or that India's involvement shielded it, and there's no mention of WTO brokering.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true according to the passage?
options: Section 122 allows a surcharge of up to 25% for one year
The India-US framework set an 18% reciprocal tariff and a $500 billion Indian purchase commitment by 2031
The Supreme Court ruling was unanimous
IEEPA was passed in 1987
questions.explain: The passage explicitly states these figures. Section 122 allows up to 15% for 150 days, not 25% for a year; the ruling was 6-3, not unanimous; and IEEPA was passed in 1977, not 1987.

questions.q: The passage mentions Article 265 of the Indian Constitution only briefly. Which of the following best describes what Article 265 states, based on general constitutional knowledge?
options: No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law
All taxes must be approved by the President personally
States cannot levy any taxes without Union government approval
Customs duties are exempt from parliamentary oversight
questions.explain: Article 265 states 'No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law,' India's own textual check on arbitrary executive taxation, paralleling the US case discussed in the passage. This requires outside knowledge the passage only gestures at with its final sentence.

passages.title: Bangladesh votes after the fall
passages.passage:
Bangladesh went to the polls on February 12, 2026 for the first time since the student-led uprising of July-August 2024 forced Sheikh Hasina, prime minister for a continuous fifteen years, to resign and flee to India. The result was a landslide: the Bangladesh Nationalist Party, led by Tarique Rahman, won 209 of 299 elected seats in the Jatiya Sangsad, while Jamaat-e-Islami, contesting independently rather than in a BNP-led coalition as in past elections, took 68 seats to become the largest opposition force.

Tarique Rahman's path back to power closes a loop three decades in the making. His father, Ziaur Rahman, founded the BNP and served as President until his assassination in 1981; his mother, Khaleda Zia, led the party through a long rivalry against Hasina that Bangladeshis call the 'Battle of the Begums.' Tarique himself spent years in London facing corruption charges he called politically motivated, returning only after Hasina's Awami League was barred from contesting this election by the interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, who had overseen the transition since August 2024.

That transition carried a harder edge than a change of government usually does. An International Crimes Tribunal in Dhaka convicted Hasina in absentia in November 2025 for crimes against humanity connected to the 2024 crackdown on protesters, in which UN estimates put the death toll above 1,400. Modi telephoned Rahman to congratulate him, a call diplomatically necessary given how central Bangladesh is to India's eastern neighbourhood, but one made carefully: the BNP has historically been viewed in Delhi as less accommodating of Indian interests than the Awami League, and unresolved issues like the Teesta river water-sharing dispute will now need fresh negotiation with a party India knows less well.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Bangladesh's 2026 election was a routine democratic exercise with no wider significance
The BNP's landslide win caps a generational family rivalry and reopens uncertain terrain in India-Bangladesh relations
Sheikh Hasina remains the most popular political figure in Bangladesh
Jamaat-e-Islami won the most seats in the election
questions.explain: The passage frames the win as closing 'a loop three decades in the making' through the Rahman-Zia-Hasina rivalry, while also flagging diplomatic uncertainty for India. Jamaat won 68 seats, not the most (ruling out D), and the passage gives no evidence for C.

questions.q: Why does the passage suggest India's congratulatory call to Rahman was diplomatically delicate?
options: Because Rahman had never held any political office before
Because the BNP has historically been viewed as less accommodating of Indian interests than the Awami League
Because Modi had previously supported Jamaat-e-Islami
Because Bangladesh is not a neighbouring country to India
questions.explain: The passage directly states the BNP 'has historically been viewed in Delhi as less accommodating of Indian interests than the Awami League,' which explains the delicacy. The other options are factually unsupported or incorrect.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus?
options: It permanently replaced Bangladesh's electoral system with an appointed legislature
It oversaw a transition that included barring the Awami League from contesting the 2026 election
It was led by a member of the BNP
It refused to hold any elections during its tenure
questions.explain: The passage states Tarique returned 'after Hasina's Awami League was barred from contesting this election by the interim government led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus.' The government did organise an election, ruling out D, and Yunus is not described as a BNP member.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: Ziaur Rahman was assassinated while serving as Prime Minister
The International Crimes Tribunal convicted Hasina in absentia in November 2025
Tarique Rahman never faced any legal charges
The BNP contested this election in coalition with Jamaat-e-Islami
questions.explain: The passage states this directly. Ziaur Rahman was President, not Prime Minister, when assassinated; Tarique faced corruption charges (even if he called them politically motivated); and Jamaat contested independently, not in coalition with the BNP.

questions.q: The passage refers to the Teesta river dispute without fully explaining it. Based on general knowledge, the Teesta dispute is primarily about what?
options: Maritime boundary demarcation in the Bay of Bengal
Sharing of river water between India and Bangladesh
Border fencing along the India-Bangladesh frontier
Trade tariffs on jute exports
questions.explain: The Teesta dispute concerns sharing the waters of the Teesta river between the two countries, a long-pending issue since a 2011 draft agreement collapsed, testing outside static knowledge the passage only names in passing.

passages.title: A month after Caracas
passages.passage:
One month after a US military operation captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro on January 3, 2026, and flew him to New York to face narcoterrorism charges, CNN's reporters found a country suspended between old fear and unclear hope. Vice President Delcy Rodriguez had stepped into the acting presidency and begun releasing political prisoners, a process that would free 621 people by early March according to the NGO Foro Penal, with more than 500 still detained. Wages, though sanctions had begun easing and oil money was trickling back, still barely covered the cost of food.

The operation's American defenders reached, at least rhetorically, for the Monroe Doctrine of 1823, President James Monroe's declaration to Congress that European powers should not interfere in the Western Hemisphere, a doctrine later expanded by Theodore Roosevelt's 1904 Corollary into a claimed US right to actively intervene in Latin American states to enforce order. Maduro's government, and Hugo Chavez's before him, had for decades invoked a different symbol: Simon Bolivar, the independence leader who liberated much of northern South America from Spain, in whose honour Chavez renamed the country the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela in 1999.

The country's economic weight complicates easy narratives on either side. Venezuela was a founding member of OPEC in 1960, alongside Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, and Saudi Arabia, and holds the world's largest proven oil reserves, yet years of sanctions, sharply tightened from 2019, had already gutted output before Maduro's capture. Regionally, the Organization of American States split over how to characterise events, with some member states welcoming Maduro's removal and others condemning what they saw as a familiar pattern of intervention.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Venezuela's economic recovery is complete now that Maduro has been removed
A month after Maduro's capture, Venezuela remains caught between competing historical narratives and an uncertain economic reality
The Monroe Doctrine has never been invoked since 1823
OPEC expelled Venezuela after Maduro's capture
questions.explain: The passage's opening frames Venezuela as 'suspended between old fear and unclear hope,' and the body develops both the political-symbolic tension (Monroe Doctrine vs Bolivar) and the unresolved economic hardship. No claim of full recovery or OPEC expulsion appears.

questions.q: According to the passage, how does the Roosevelt Corollary relate to the original Monroe Doctrine?
options: It repealed the Monroe Doctrine entirely
It was issued before the Monroe Doctrine
It expanded the Monroe Doctrine into a claimed right of active US intervention in Latin America
It applied only to European countries, not the US
questions.explain: The passage states the Corollary 'expanded' the original doctrine 'into a claimed US right to actively intervene in Latin American states.' It came later (1904 versus 1823), not before, ruling out B, and the passage gives no basis for A or D.

questions.q: What can be inferred about why Chavez renamed Venezuela the 'Bolivarian Republic'?
options: To align the country's identity with Simon Bolivar's legacy as an anti-imperialist independence figure
Because Bolivar personally founded modern Venezuela's government in 1999
To comply with an OAS requirement
Because OPEC required the name change for membership
questions.explain: The passage connects the renaming to invoking Bolivar's legacy as a counter to US-aligned framing, consistent with Chavez's and Maduro's anti-imperialist political project. Bolivar died in 1830, long before 1999, ruling out B; no OAS or OPEC naming requirement is mentioned.

questions.q: Which of the following is stated as true in the passage?
options: Venezuela's oil output had already declined sharply before Maduro's capture due to sanctions
The Organization of American States unanimously condemned Maduro's capture
Foro Penal reported zero political prisoners released as of March 2026
OPEC was founded in 1970
questions.explain: The passage states 'years of sanctions...had already gutted output before Maduro's capture.' The OAS was described as 'split,' not unanimous; Foro Penal reported 621 released, not zero; and OPEC was founded in 1960, not 1970.

questions.q: The passage does not name all of OPEC's founding members explicitly stated. Based on the passage and general knowledge, which of these was a founding OPEC member in 1960?
options: Nigeria
Kuwait
United Arab Emirates
Qatar
questions.explain: The passage names Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and Venezuela as OPEC's 1960 founders. Nigeria, the UAE, and Qatar joined OPEC only in later decades.

passages.title: Two cutoff dates, one courtroom
passages.passage:
Nearly two years after more than 200 petitions had piled up before it, the Supreme Court on February 19, 2026 finally began substantive hearings on the constitutionality of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019. The Court directed that pan-India objections to the law be argued first, before turning separately to challenges specific to Assam and Tripura, an ordering that reflects how differently the CAA lands depending on where in India one asks the question.

At the national level, the core objection rests on Article 14's guarantee of equality before the law: the CAA fast-tracks citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan who arrived before December 31, 2014, while leaving out Muslims from the same countries and the same route, a distinction petitioners argue cannot survive equal-protection scrutiny no matter how the government frames its purpose of protecting persecuted minorities.

In Assam, the objection is older and more specific. The Assam Accord of 1985, which ended a six-year agitation known as the Assam Movement, fixed March 24, 1971 as the cutoff date for detecting and expelling foreigners, a date written into Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955. The CAA's cutoff, thirteen years later, effectively lets in as citizens people the Assam Accord's own framework would have classified as illegal migrants, which is why Assamese groups argue the 2019 law overrides a negotiated political settlement rather than merely adding a new citizenship category.

The case sits beside, but is legally distinct from, the National Register of Citizens exercise last updated for Assam in 2019, which excluded over 19 lakh applicants and remains largely unimplemented. The CAA grants citizenship; the NRC verifies who already holds it, a distinction students routinely blur but examiners do not.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The CAA is unconstitutional and will certainly be struck down
The CAA raises both a general equality objection and a distinct, older Assam-specific objection rooted in the 1985 Accord
The NRC and CAA are the same legal process
Only Muslims are affected by the Citizenship Act, 1955
questions.explain: The passage structures itself around exactly this distinction: a national Article 14 argument and a separate, historically rooted Assam argument. It does not predict an outcome (ruling out A), and it explicitly separates CAA from NRC (ruling out C).

questions.q: Why do Assamese groups object to the CAA's cutoff date specifically, according to the passage?
options: Because the CAA has no cutoff date at all
Because the CAA's 2014 cutoff would grant citizenship to people the 1971 Assam Accord cutoff would classify as illegal migrants
Because the Assam Accord was struck down by the Supreme Court
Because Assam does not recognise the Citizenship Act, 1955
questions.explain: The passage explains the CAA's 2014 cutoff is 'thirteen years later' than the Accord's 1971 cutoff, letting in people the older framework would have excluded. There is no claim the Accord was struck down or that Assam rejects the 1955 Act.

questions.q: What can be inferred about why the Court chose to hear pan-India issues before Assam and Tripura-specific ones?
options: Because Assam and Tripura's objections are legally irrelevant
Because the general equality question and the state-specific historical questions are analytically distinct and may be easier to resolve separately
Because the Assam Accord is no longer valid law
Because Tripura withdrew its petition
questions.explain: The passage frames the ordering as reflecting how 'differently the CAA lands' at the national versus state level, implying the Court is separating analytically distinct questions rather than dismissing either. No textual basis supports the other options.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true according to the passage?
options: The NRC exercise granted citizenship to over 19 lakh people
The Assam Accord's cutoff date is codified in Section 6A of the Citizenship Act, 1955
The CAA applies to migrants from any country without restriction
Fewer than 50 petitions challenge the CAA's constitutionality
questions.explain: The passage states this directly. The NRC excluded, not granted citizenship to, over 19 lakh applicants; the CAA applies only to migrants from Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Afghanistan; and the passage cites over 200 pending petitions, not fewer than 50.

questions.q: The passage mentions Article 14 as the primary ground of challenge but does not elaborate on it. Which of the following best states what Article 14 guarantees?
options: Freedom of speech and expression
Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws
Protection of life and personal liberty
Freedom to practise any religion
questions.explain: Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws, distinct from Article 19 (speech), Article 21 (life and liberty), and Article 25 (religious freedom), a distinction requiring outside constitutional knowledge.

passages.title: From Bletchley to Bharat Mandapam
passages.passage:
When 92 countries and organisations signed the New Delhi Declaration on AI Impact on February 19, 2026, the document capped a six-day summit at Bharat Mandapam that drew roughly six lakh in-person attendees. It was also, in a smaller sense, the fourth stop on a journey that began at Bletchley Park in the United Kingdom in November 2023, continued through Seoul in May 2024 and Paris in February 2025, and arrived in New Delhi with a change of name from 'Safety' to 'Impact', a shift meant to signal a move from restricting AI's risks toward capturing its economic upside, particularly for countries outside the small circle of nations building frontier AI models.

The Declaration structures itself around seven pillars it calls Chakras: democratised access to AI resources, economic growth, secure systems, scientific research, social empowerment, human capital, and energy-efficient AI. From these, concrete initiatives followed, among them a Charter for the Democratic Diffusion of AI meant to give developing countries affordable access to compute and foundational models they currently cannot build or afford to train themselves.

That compute gap is not abstract. Training a frontier AI model requires vast clusters of specialised chips, made almost exclusively by a handful of firms, and access to them has become as consequential a strategic asset as oil was in the twentieth century. Unlike the European Union's AI Act, a binding law in force since August 2024 that classifies systems by risk tier, the New Delhi Declaration carries no enforcement mechanism; it is a political statement of intent, closer in character to a G20 communique than a treaty. Whether its Chakras translate into functioning institutions, the Global AI Impact Commons and Trusted AI Commons among them, will depend on follow-through no summit declaration can itself guarantee.

questions.q: What is the central point the passage makes about the New Delhi Declaration's legal status?
options: It is a binding treaty enforceable in international courts
It is a non-binding political statement, unlike the EU's binding AI Act
It replaced the EU AI Act entirely
It has the same enforcement mechanism as the Bletchley Declaration
questions.explain: The passage explicitly contrasts the Declaration, 'a political statement of intent,' with the EU AI Act, 'a binding law.' It does not claim the Declaration replaced anything, and it does not describe the Bletchley Declaration's enforcement mechanism for comparison.

questions.q: Why does the passage compare access to AI compute with oil in the twentieth century?
options: Because AI chips are made from petroleum products
To illustrate that compute access has become a comparably significant strategic resource
Because oil-producing nations now control most AI chip production
To argue that AI will replace oil as an energy source
questions.explain: The comparison is rhetorical, meant to convey how strategically consequential compute access has become, not a literal claim about chip composition, oil nations' control, or energy replacement, none of which the passage states.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the summit's rename from 'Safety' to 'Impact'?
options: It reflects a shift in emphasis from restricting AI risk toward capturing AI's economic benefits for a wider set of countries
It means safety concerns were abandoned entirely
It was a purely cosmetic change with no substantive meaning
It occurred at the Paris summit, not New Delhi
questions.explain: The passage states the renaming was 'meant to signal a move from restricting AI's risks toward capturing its economic upside,' directly supporting this inference. It does not suggest safety was abandoned, dismiss the change as cosmetic, or misplace it at Paris rather than New Delhi.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: The New Delhi summit was the second in a series that began in 2023
The Declaration was signed by exactly 50 countries
The summit preceding New Delhi's was held in Paris in February 2025
The EU AI Act has not yet come into force
questions.explain: The passage states the sequence ran 'Bletchley Park...Seoul...and Paris in February 2025' before New Delhi. The Declaration had 92 signatories, not 50; New Delhi was the fourth summit, not the second; and the EU AI Act has been in force since August 2024.

questions.q: The passage does not name who founded OpenAI. Based on general knowledge, in what year and by whom was OpenAI founded?
options: 2015, by Sam Altman and Elon Musk among others
2010, by Larry Page and Sergey Brin
2019, by Sundar Pichai
2012, by Mark Zuckerberg
questions.explain: OpenAI was founded in December 2015 as a non-profit by Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and others, a fact the passage's topic connects to but does not state directly, testing outside static knowledge about the AI industry's key players.

passages.title: One definition, two decades of consequences
passages.passage:
Parliament passed the Industrial Relations Code (Amendment) Bill on February 11, 2026, confirming that three predecessor labour statutes, the Trade Unions Act of 1926, the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act of 1946, and the Industrial Disputes Act of 1947, had stood repealed since November 21, 2025, the day the four consolidated labour codes took effect. Five days later, the Supreme Court revived a nine-judge Constitution Bench reference, dormant for years, to settle a question the repeal did not resolve: what exactly counts as an 'industry' under Section 2(j) of the old Industrial Disputes Act.

The question has a long history. In 1978, a seven-judge bench in Bangalore Water Supply and Sewerage Board v. A. Rajappa gave 'industry' an expansive reading, covering almost any organised activity involving cooperation between employer and employee to produce goods or services, sweeping in hospitals, universities, and charitable institutions that might not obviously look like factories or businesses. Critics argued the reading was too broad, and the case was referred to a larger bench for reconsideration, a reference that then sat unaddressed for decades while lower courts continued applying the 1978 standard.

The stakes are not merely academic. Whether an institution counts as an 'industry' determines whether its workers can legally form recognised unions, bargain collectively, or go on strike under labour law protections. The new Industrial Relations Code, 2020, which now governs these questions in place of the repealed 1947 Act, carries forward a definition structurally similar to the one Bangalore Water Supply interpreted, meaning the Court's eventual ruling will shape how the new code applies to precisely the same range of institutions the old case debated, nearly half a century on.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: The repeal of old labour laws in 2025 fully resolved the definition of 'industry'
A decades-old unresolved legal question about the definition of 'industry' remains consequential even after the labour codes replaced the old law
The Bangalore Water Supply case has been overruled
Only factories qualify as 'industries' under Indian law
questions.explain: The passage's structure moves from the 2025 repeal to the unresolved 1978 precedent to its continuing relevance under the new Code, making clear the repeal did not settle the question. Nothing in the passage says Bangalore Water Supply was overruled, and the 1978 case's holding was broader than 'only factories'.

questions.q: According to the passage, why does the classification of an institution as an 'industry' matter practically?
options: It determines tax rates for the institution
It determines whether workers there can legally unionise, bargain collectively, or strike under labour law
It determines whether the institution can receive government subsidies
It has no practical consequence, only symbolic value
questions.explain: The passage states directly that the classification 'determines whether an institution's workers can legally form recognised unions, bargain collectively, or go on strike.' No mention is made of tax rates or subsidies.

questions.q: What can be inferred about why the Supreme Court revived the nine-judge bench reference in February 2026?
options: Because the 1978 ruling had just been issued
Because the new Industrial Relations Code carries forward a similarly broad definition, so the old unresolved question remains live
Because the labour codes eliminated the need for any definition of 'industry'
Because the Trade Unions Act, 1926 was never repealed
questions.explain: The passage notes the new Code 'carries forward a definition structurally similar to the one Bangalore Water Supply interpreted,' meaning the old question persists under new law. The 1978 ruling long preceded 2026, and the passage confirms the Trade Unions Act was in fact repealed.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: The Bangalore Water Supply case was decided by a nine-judge bench
The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 was repealed effective November 21, 2025
The Industrial Relations Code (Amendment) Bill was passed before the labour codes took effect
The reference to a larger bench was resolved within a year of the 1978 judgment
questions.explain: The passage states the repeal took effect November 21, 2025. Bangalore Water Supply was decided by a seven-judge bench, not nine; the Amendment Bill passed in February 2026, after the codes took effect in November 2025; and the reference 'sat unaddressed for decades,' not within a year.

questions.q: The passage refers to hospitals and charitable institutions as examples debated under the 'industry' definition. Which constitutional provision on the Directive Principles is most commonly cited alongside labour welfare debates like this one?
options: Article 43, living wage and humane working conditions
Article 32, right to constitutional remedies
Article 370, special status
Article 356, President's Rule
questions.explain: Article 43 of the Directive Principles calls for securing a living wage and humane working conditions, a provision courts often invoke when interpreting labour welfare statutes broadly, which is exactly the interpretive question this passage describes. The other articles concern unrelated subjects.

passages.title: Talking mechanisms without a settled line
passages.passage:
Through early 2026, India and China worked to consolidate a diplomatic thaw that traces back to the deadliest border clash between the two countries since 1967: the June 2020 confrontation in the Galwan Valley, which killed 20 Indian soldiers and froze high-level engagement for years afterward. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi's visit to New Delhi, where he met National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Prime Minister Modi, produced an agreement to establish a general-level talks mechanism covering the eastern and central sectors of the roughly 3,488-kilometre Line of Actual Control, building on the Special Representatives dialogue Doval has run opposite Wang Yi since 2003.

The two countries also agreed to support each other's diplomatic calendars for 2026, with China backing India's turn to host the BRICS summit. Yet External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, in public remarks through this period, kept returning to one formulation: that peace and tranquillity at the border is a precondition, not a byproduct, of normalised relations, a phrasing meant to resist any suggestion that economic and diplomatic ties could deepen independently of an actual border settlement.

The LAC itself is not a formally demarcated international border. It is a loosely defined line of military control that emerged after the 1962 Sino-Indian War, distinct from the McMahon Line, drawn at the 1914 Simla Convention to demarcate specifically the eastern sector, a line China has never accepted. Disengagement at friction points like Depsang and Demchok, agreed after an October 2024 Modi-Xi meeting at the Kazan BRICS summit, continued into 2026, but disengagement, meaning troops pulling back from face-to-face contact, is a narrower and more limited step than de-escalation, meaning an actual reduction in troop numbers along the frontier, which remains unresolved.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: India and China have fully resolved their border dispute
India and China are building talks mechanisms and diplomatic cooperation even though the underlying border dispute remains unresolved
The LAC and the McMahon Line are the same thing
China has accepted the McMahon Line as the official border
questions.explain: The passage shows procedural and diplomatic progress, talks mechanisms, summit cooperation, alongside an explicit statement that the border itself remains unsettled and that China has never accepted the McMahon Line, directly contradicting options C and D.

questions.q: According to the passage, what is the difference between 'disengagement' and 'de-escalation'?
options: They are identical terms used interchangeably
Disengagement means troops pulling back from face-to-face contact points; de-escalation means an actual reduction in troop numbers along the frontier
De-escalation happened first, followed by disengagement
Disengagement applies only to the western sector
questions.explain: The passage defines both terms precisely and in that order of scope: disengagement is the narrower, already-achieved step, while de-escalation, broader troop reduction, 'remains unresolved.' No sector restriction or reversed sequence is stated.

questions.q: What can be inferred about Jaishankar's repeated formulation on border peace?
options: He believes normalisation can proceed even without border peace
He is signalling that India will not treat diplomatic or economic warmth as a substitute for resolving the border dispute
He opposes all talks mechanisms with China
He believes the LAC dispute has already been resolved
questions.explain: The passage states his phrasing was 'meant to resist any suggestion that economic and diplomatic ties could deepen independently of an actual border settlement,' precisely the position in option B. He is not shown opposing talks mechanisms, which the passage describes India engaging in.

questions.q: Which of the following is true according to the passage?
options: The Galwan Valley clash occurred in June 2020 and was the deadliest India-China border confrontation since 1967
The McMahon Line was drawn in 1962
China has formally accepted the McMahon Line
The Special Representatives dialogue began in 2020
questions.explain: The passage states this directly. The McMahon Line was drawn in 1914 at the Simla Convention, not 1962; China has never accepted it; and the Special Representatives dialogue has run since 2003, not 2020.

questions.q: The passage does not elaborate on the Special Representatives dialogue's origin. Based on general knowledge, what is the primary purpose of this dialogue?
options: To negotiate trade tariffs between India and China
To negotiate a political framework and eventual settlement of the India-China border dispute
To coordinate joint military exercises
To manage visa and travel agreements
questions.explain: The Special Representatives dialogue, running since 2003 between India's NSA and China's Foreign Minister, exists specifically to negotiate political parameters for an eventual border settlement, not trade, military exercises, or visas.
